did_you_know.text: Did you know? The psalm’s title includes two details: “For the choir director” and “A psalm of David.”

Did you know? In this verse, the question “How long?” appears twice. It expresses the speaker’s sense of prolonged waiting and his questions about being forgotten and having the LORD hide His face from him.
Did you know? In this verse, the question “How long?” also appears twice. Thus, the phrase appears four times in verses 2–3, emphasizing the intensity of the distress.
Did you know? The speaker describes three sources of difficulty: having to devise plans, continual sorrow in his heart, and an enemy who exalts himself over him.
Did you know? In this verse, the speaker makes three direct requests: “Look at me,” “Answer me,” and “Light up my eyes,” asking the LORD for attention, a response, and light.

Did you know? The expression “Light up my eyes” is directly connected to the request “lest I sleep the sleep of death.” This sequence suggests that the lighting of the eyes is a request for deliverance from grave danger.

Did you know? The speaker fears that his enemy will say, “I have overcome him,” and that his foes will rejoice when he falls. The verse presents not only the danger itself, but also the fear that his opponents will celebrate his downfall.

Did you know? The final verse marks a sharp transition: after describing his distress, the speaker declares, “But I have trusted in Your steadfast love,” followed by joy in God’s salvation and a commitment to sing to the LORD.
